art-iii-sec-1.x:
Government may not take away your life, your freedom, or your property unless it follows a fair process and has a fair reason. It also may not treat people differently without a real, relevant basis.

Due process has two sides. Procedural due process asks how the government acted: notice and a chance to be heard before an impartial body. Substantive due process asks whether the law or act itself is fair and reasonable. Equal protection does not require identical treatment. It forbids arbitrary classification.
k: Procedural due process: notice, an opportunity to be heard, an impartial tribunal with jurisdiction, and a decision based on evidence.
Substantive due process: a lawful purpose (public interest) and lawful means (reasonably necessary, not unduly oppressive).
Valid classification (Cayat test): substantial distinctions; germane to the purpose of the law; not limited to existing conditions only; applies equally to all members of the class.
The guarantee protects natural and juridical persons, citizens and aliens alike.
art-iii-sec-1.w: It is the master limit on police power: the State may regulate liberty and property for the common good, but only by fair means and for real reasons.
t: The Bill of Rights restrains the State, not private persons (People v. Marti).
Administrative due process does not always require a trial-type hearing; the chance to explain one’s side, even in writing, can suffice.
Strict scrutiny, intermediate scrutiny and the rational-basis test apply to different classifications. Fundamental rights and suspect classes get strict scrutiny.
q: Give the four requisites of a valid classification.
Distinguish procedural from substantive due process with one example each.
Does the clause protect a corporation’s property?

d.h: A law penalizing members of non-Christian tribes for possessing liquor not native to them was upheld. The Court laid down the four requisites of a reasonable classification: substantial distinctions, germane to the purpose of the law, not limited to existing conditions, and equal application to all members of the class.
d.r: The standard test for equal protection.

d.n: White Light Corporation v. City of Manila
d.h: A Manila ordinance barring short-time admission and wash-up rates in motels was struck down. Its aim of curbing illicit sex was legitimate, but banning the rates swept in lawful conduct and intruded on liberty and private enterprise. The means were unreasonable and unduly oppressive, so the ordinance failed substantive due process.
d.r: Applies the lawful-purpose / lawful-means test to police-power measures.

art-iii-sec-2.x: You have a right not to be searched, or to have your things or yourself seized, unreasonably. As a rule, the police need a warrant. Only a judge can issue it, and only after personally examining the complainant and witnesses under oath and finding probable cause. The warrant must describe exactly the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized.
k: The right is personal and may be waived, but a waiver must be clear and voluntary.

Requisites of a valid warrant: (1) probable cause; (2) determined personally by the judge; (3) after examination under oath or affirmation of the complainant and witnesses; (4) particular description of the place, persons or things.
General warrants are void.
Evidence obtained in violation of Sec. 2 is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding (Sec. 3(2)).

Recognized warrantless searches: incident to a lawful arrest; plain view; moving vehicles; consented searches; customs searches; stop-and-frisk; exigent and emergency circumstances; checkpoints within limits.
art-iii-sec-2.w: It keeps the power to invade homes and persons under the control of a neutral judge, not the officer who wants the evidence.
t: Only a judge, not a prosecutor or administrative officer, may issue search or arrest warrants. The exception is deportation orders by the Commissioner of Immigration to carry out a final order.

For arrest warrants, the judge may rely on the prosecutor’s report and supporting documents. For search warrants, the judge must personally examine the applicant and witnesses with searching questions.
A search incident to arrest presupposes a lawful arrest first. It cannot justify the arrest after the fact.
q: List the requisites of a valid search warrant.
Name five recognized warrantless searches.
Does the exclusionary rule apply to evidence seized by a private individual acting on his own?

d.h: Warrants describing the offense only as violations of tax and banking laws and the RPC, and authorizing seizure of practically all business records, were general warrants and void. Evidence seized under them is inadmissible. The Court abandoned the contrary Moncado rule.
d.r: The leading case on the particularity requirement and the exclusionary rule.

d.h: A forwarding company’s proprietor opened a package and found marijuana, then turned it over to agents. The evidence was admissible because the search was by a private person acting on his own, not by the State. The Bill of Rights restrains government.
d.r: Shows that the guarantee applies only to government action.

art-iii-sec-3.x: Your private communications and letters are protected. The government may open or intercept them only with a court order, or when public safety or order requires it as the law prescribes. Anything obtained in violation of this section, or of Section 2, cannot be used as evidence against anyone, in any proceeding.
k: Intrusion is allowed only (a) upon lawful order of the court, or (b) when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law.
Paragraph (2) contains the exclusionary rule for Sections 2 and 3: inadmissible “for any purpose in any proceeding.”
Related statutes: RA 4200 (Anti-Wiretapping), RA 10173 (Data Privacy), RA 9995 (Anti-Photo and Video Voyeurism).
art-iii-sec-3.w: Privacy of communication protects freedom of thought and association; people speak and write differently when they fear being overheard.
t: The constitutional exclusionary rule binds the State. But privacy statutes such as RA 4200 bind private persons too. A recording made secretly by a party to the conversation is still illegal under RA 4200 (Ramirez v. CA).
Even between spouses, evidence taken by force or stealth from the other spouse’s papers is inadmissible (Zulueta v. CA).
q: When may privacy of communication be intruded upon?
Is a secret recording by one of the parties to a phone call admissible?

d.h: A wife forcibly took her husband’s private letters and photos from his clinic to use in legal separation and disbarment cases. The documents were inadmissible. Marriage does not waive a spouse’s right to privacy of communication and correspondence.
d.r: The exclusionary rule applied in a dispute between private parties.

d.h: Secretly taping a private conversation without the consent of all parties violates RA 4200, even if the person recording is a party to it. The law makes no distinction.
d.r: Read with Sec. 3: a statute can extend privacy protection to private actors.

art-iii-sec-4.x: The government may not pass laws that cut down your freedom to speak, write, publish or broadcast, or your right to gather peacefully and ask government to fix grievances. Free speech is a preferred right. It is not absolute, but any restriction must clear demanding tests.
k: Two aspects: freedom from prior restraint (censorship) and freedom from subsequent punishment.
Any system of prior restraint carries a heavy presumption of unconstitutionality.
Content-based restrictions get strict scrutiny and the clear-and-present-danger test. Content-neutral restrictions get intermediate scrutiny (the O’Brien test).
Unprotected speech includes obscenity, defamation, fighting words, and incitement to imminent lawless action.
Assembly: permits may regulate time, place and manner but cannot be denied because of the message (BP 880; the maximum-tolerance policy).
art-iii-sec-4.w: Self-government needs the free flow of ideas; truth is best tested in the open market of ideas.
t: Content-neutral regulation is not the same as content-based regulation, and the test changes with it.
Election-period regulation of speech by private persons on their own property can be unconstitutional (Diocese of Bacolod).
A public official must prove actual malice to recover for defamation relating to official conduct.
q: What is the presumption against prior restraint?
Distinguish the clear-and-present-danger test from the dangerous-tendency test.
Give three categories of unprotected speech.

d.h: Official warnings by the DOJ Secretary and the NTC that airing the “Garci” tapes could violate the law and lead to cancelled broadcast permits were struck down as unconstitutional prior restraint. Content-based restraints are presumed invalid and the government bears a heavy burden of justification.
d.r: The leading modern case on prior restraint.

d.h: COMELEC could not order a church to remove an oversized tarpaulin about candidates’ RH Law votes, posted on church property. It was the speech of a private citizen on a matter of public concern, not election propaganda by a candidate, and the size limit was a content-based restriction that failed strict scrutiny.
d.r: Applies Sec. 4 to election regulation and private speech.

art-iii-sec-5.x: The government may not set up an official religion, and it may not stop people from practising their faith. No religious test can be required to vote or to hold public office or exercise civil and political rights.
k: Two clauses: non-establishment and free exercise.
Free exercise covers freedom to believe, which is absolute, and freedom to act on belief, which may be regulated.
Philippine approach: benevolent neutrality and accommodation. A burden on religious exercise needs a compelling state interest pursued by the least restrictive means.
Related: Art. II, Sec. 6 (separation of Church and State); Art. VI, Sec. 29(2) (no public money for religion).
art-iii-sec-5.w: It protects conscience and keeps government from taking sides among faiths.
t: Benevolent neutrality is not the same as strict separation. Philippine courts may grant exemptions from general laws.
Religious instruction in public schools is allowed under Art. XIV, Sec. 3(3) on the conditions stated there.
q: State the compelling-state-interest test under benevolent neutrality.
Can students be expelled for refusing to salute the flag on religious grounds?

d.h: A court interpreter lived with a man not her husband under a “declaration of pledging faithfulness” approved by her congregation. The Court adopted benevolent neutrality. Since the State showed no compelling interest that the least restrictive means required, she was not held administratively liable for disgraceful and immoral conduct.
d.r: The controlling framework for free-exercise exemptions.

d.n: Ebralinag v. Division Superintendent of Schools of Cebu
d.h: Expelling Jehovah’s Witness students for refusing to salute the flag and sing the anthem violated free exercise. Their refusal posed no grave and imminent danger to public safety.
d.r: Free exercise prevails absent a grave and present danger.

art-iii-sec-6.x: You may live where you want and move house within the limits the law sets. Only a court order can impair that. You may also travel. That right can be limited only by law and only for national security, public safety or public health.
k: Liberty of abode may be impaired only upon lawful order of the court.
The right to travel may be impaired only by law, on the grounds of national security, public safety or public health.
Courts may restrict an accused’s travel as a condition of bail, under their inherent power.
art-iii-sec-6.w: Movement is basic to liberty; restrictions must come from the people’s representatives (a law) or a judge, not from executive whim.
t: An executive circular alone cannot authorize hold-departure or watchlist orders (Genuino v. De Lima).
Marcos v. Manglapus upheld a ban on a former president’s return on the basis of the President’s residual powers. It is often treated as sui generis.
q: Who may impair liberty of abode? Who may impair the right to travel, and on what grounds?

d.h: DOJ Department Circular No. 41, which allowed the Secretary to issue watchlist and hold-departure orders, was declared unconstitutional. The right to travel may be impaired only by a law on the stated grounds, and no law authorized the DOJ to do so.
d.r: Restrictions on travel need statutory basis.

art-iii-sec-7.x: You have a right to information on matters of public concern. That includes official records, documents on official acts and decisions, and government research data used as a basis for policy, subject to limits set by law.
k: Self-executing; enforceable by mandamus.

Covers matters of public concern and public interest. Some information is exempt: national security, diplomatic negotiations, executive privilege, trade secrets, privacy, matters under investigation and similar categories.
Related: Art. II, Sec. 28 (full public disclosure policy).
art-iii-sec-7.w: Citizens cannot hold government accountable for what they cannot see.
t: The right is subject to reasonable regulation of the manner of access, but not to denial at the custodian’s discretion.
Information on negotiations before a final agreement may be protected. The final terms are not (Chavez v. PEA).
q: What remedy enforces the right to information?
Name four recognized limits.

d.h: A citizen may compel the CSC, by mandamus, to disclose whether particular sanitarians passed the civil service exam. The right is self-executing, and any citizen has standing because it is a public right.
d.r: Establishes standing and the mandamus remedy.

d.h: The public is entitled to information on negotiations leading to a government contract involving public property, at least at the stage of definite propositions. The Court also voided the transfer of reclaimed submerged lands to a private corporation.
d.r: Scope of “official acts” and the timing of disclosure.

art-iii-sec-8.x: People in both the public and private sectors may form unions, associations or societies for purposes not contrary to law. The government may not cut down this right.
k: Purposes must not be contrary to law.
Government employees may organize (Art. IX-B, Sec. 2(5)), but they have no right to strike.
Related: Art. XIII, Sec. 3 (rights of workers); the Labor Code on self-organization.
art-iii-sec-8.w: Collective action lets individuals protect interests they could not protect alone.
t: The right to form associations does not include a right to strike for government workers.
q: Do government employees have the right to strike?

d.n: SSS Employees Association v. Court of Appeals
d.h: Government employees, including those of GOCCs with original charters, may organize but may not strike. Their terms of employment are fixed by law, not by bargaining.
d.r: Defines the limit of the right for public-sector workers.

art-iii-sec-9.x: The government may take private property, but only for public use and only after paying just compensation. That means the full and fair value of the property at the time of taking, paid within a reasonable time.
k: Requisites: (1) private property; (2) genuine necessity; (3) taking in the constitutional sense; (4) for public use; (5) payment of just compensation; (6) observance of due process.
“Taking” includes a substantial burden on use even without transfer of title (e.g., easements that deprive normal use).
“Public use” is construed broadly as public advantage or benefit.
Just compensation is a judicial function. Legislative or executive valuations bind the courts only as guides.
Under RA 10752, initial deposit or payment rules apply before the writ of possession issues.
art-iii-sec-9.w: It balances the State’s inherent power to acquire property against fairness to the owner who bears a public burden.
t: Valuation date: generally the time of taking or of filing the complaint, whichever came first.
Delay in payment may earn legal interest as damages.
Eminent domain may be delegated to LGUs (by ordinance; LGC Sec. 19) and to public utilities by law.
q: List the requisites of a valid exercise of eminent domain.
When is there “taking” without transfer of title?
Who finally determines just compensation?

d.h: Expropriating the birthplace of Felix Manalo to preserve it as a national historical landmark was for a public use. That a religious group would incidentally benefit did not defeat the public purpose.
d.r: Public use is understood broadly as public benefit.

d.h: In expropriating the NAIA Terminal 3 facilities, the government had to pay the builder the proffered value under RA 8974 before a writ of possession could issue. Rule 67’s mere deposit of assessed value did not suffice.
d.r: Payment rules before possession in infrastructure expropriation.

art-iii-sec-10.x: The legislature may not pass a law that changes the terms of existing contracts to the prejudice of a party. But all contracts are made subject to the State’s police power, so reasonable regulation for the general welfare can still affect them.
k: Applies to laws, not judicial decisions or executive acts.
Impairment means a change in the terms, or new conditions, that lessens a party’s rights.
Police power prevails: contracts are deemed to incorporate the reserved power of the State to regulate.
Franchises and licences are generally not contracts protected by this clause (Art. XII, Sec. 11).
art-iii-sec-10.w: It protects the stability of private bargains while keeping the State able to act for the common good.
t: Zoning ordinances may override restrictive covenants in deeds (Ortigas v. Feati Bank).
q: Why do police-power measures that affect contracts not violate this clause?

d.n: Ortigas & Co. v. Feati Bank and Trust Co.
d.h: A municipal resolution zoning an area as commercial and industrial prevailed over a deed restriction limiting the lots to residential use. Contracts are subject to the police power, so there was no unconstitutional impairment.
d.r: Police power versus non-impairment.

art-iii-sec-11.x: Poverty must not shut anyone out of the courts or quasi-judicial bodies, or deprive them of adequate legal help.
k: Basis for exemption of indigent litigants from docket fees (Rules of Court) and for free legal assistance (PAO, IBP).
Covers access to courts and to quasi-judicial bodies.
art-iii-sec-11.w: Equal justice is meaningless if the poor cannot get into court.
t: This right is distinct from the right to counsel of an accused under Secs. 12 and 14.
q: What practical rules implement this guarantee?

art-iii-sec-12.x: Once the police are questioning you as a suspect, you have rights. You must be told you may stay silent and may have a lawyer, preferably one you choose. If you cannot afford one, a lawyer must be given to you. You may waive these rights only in writing and with a lawyer present. No torture, force or threats may be used, and no secret detention. A confession obtained in violation of this section cannot be used against you.
k: Applies from custodial investigation: when the person is in custody or significantly deprived of freedom, and questioning focuses on him as a suspect (expanded by RA 7438 to include “inviting” a person for questioning).
Rights: to remain silent; to competent and independent counsel, preferably of his own choice; to be informed of these rights.
Waiver must be in writing and in the presence of counsel.
Exclusionary rule: confessions or admissions obtained in violation are inadmissible (par. 3).
Par. 4: penal and civil sanctions, compensation and rehabilitation for victims of torture and similar practices.
art-iii-sec-12.w: The inherently coercive setting of police custody would otherwise make confessions unreliable and involuntary.
t: Rights do not apply to spontaneous statements, or to statements made to private persons or media (absent State involvement).
A police line-up is generally not custodial investigation.
“Competent and independent” counsel excludes a lawyer with interests adverse to the accused, such as the police legal officer or a mayor.
q: When does custodial investigation begin?
How may custodial rights be waived?
Is an extrajudicial confession made to a radio reporter admissible?

d.h: A confession was inadmissible because the accused was not effectively informed of his rights and was not assisted by counsel. A perfunctory recital of rights is not enough; the warnings must be meaningful, in a language the person understands.
d.r: The quality, not just the fact, of the warning matters.

art-iii-sec-13.x: Before conviction, everyone may be released on bail, except those charged with offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua when the evidence of guilt is strong. Bail must not be excessive. Even when the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus is suspended, the right to bail stays.
k: Bail is a matter of right before conviction, except in capital offenses or those punishable by reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment when evidence of guilt is strong.
In such offenses a hearing is mandatory, and the prosecution bears the burden of showing strong evidence.
Excessive bail is prohibited.
The right survives suspension of the privilege of the writ.
art-iii-sec-13.w: The presumption of innocence: liberty before judgment is the rule; detention is the exception.
t: After conviction by the RTC of an offense not punishable by reclusion perpetua, bail becomes discretionary (Rule 114).
Bail may be granted in extradition proceedings on clear and convincing proof that the extraditee is not a flight risk (Hong Kong v. Olalia).
Humanitarian grounds may justify bail even in serious offenses (Enrile v. Sandiganbayan).
q: When is bail a matter of right? A matter of discretion? Not available?
Is a bail hearing required when the charge carries reclusion perpetua?

d.n: Government of Hong Kong SAR v. Olalia
d.h: A potential extraditee may be admitted to bail. Extradition is not a criminal proceeding, but liberty is still at stake, and international human-rights norms apply. The extraditee must show by clear and convincing evidence that he is not a flight risk.
d.r: Extends the bail guarantee beyond criminal cases.

d.h: An accused charged with plunder was granted bail because of his advanced age, frail health and the low risk that he would flee. Bail exists to guarantee appearance, not to punish.
d.r: Bail may rest on humanitarian considerations.

art-iii-sec-14.x: No one may be tried for a crime without due process of law. In every criminal prosecution the accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty. He is entitled to be heard personally and by counsel, to be told the nature of the charge, and to a speedy, impartial and public trial. He may meet the witnesses face to face and compel the attendance of witnesses and evidence in his favour. Trial may continue in his absence after arraignment if he was notified and his failure to appear is unjustifiable.
k: Presumption of innocence: guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.
Right to be heard by himself and counsel.
Right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation (the facts alleged, not the label, control).
Speedy, impartial and public trial.
Confrontation and compulsory process.
Trial in absentia: after arraignment, with due notice and unjustified absence.
art-iii-sec-14.w: It equalizes the contest between the State, with all its resources, and the individual.
t: Trial in absentia requires prior arraignment. The accused may still be compelled to appear for identification.
The description of the acts in the information, not its caption, determines the offense charged.
q: List the requisites of trial in absentia.
What determines the offense charged — the caption or the allegations?

d.h: Conviction on a plea of guilty entered without counsel, where the court did not inform the accused of his right to a lawyer, violated due process. The case was remanded for proper arraignment and trial.
d.r: The court’s duty to ensure the right to counsel at arraignment.

art-iii-sec-15.x: The privilege of the writ of habeas corpus — the right to have a court look into why someone is detained — may be suspended only for invasion or rebellion, and only when public safety requires it.
k: Grounds: invasion or rebellion, when public safety requires it.

Read with Art. VII, Sec. 18: the President may suspend for up to 60 days; Congress may revoke or extend; the Supreme Court may review the sufficiency of the factual basis within 30 days of a petition.

Suspension applies only to persons judicially charged with rebellion or offenses inherent in or directly connected with invasion. Anyone arrested must be judicially charged within three days or released.
art-iii-sec-15.w: Habeas corpus is the great writ of liberty; its suspension is an emergency measure with tight limits.
t: The writ itself is never suspended — only its privilege.
The right to bail is not impaired by suspension (Sec. 13).
q: On what grounds may the privilege be suspended, and who may review the basis?

d.h: The Court may inquire into whether the President’s suspension of the privilege had a sufficient factual basis, abandoning the earlier view that the matter was a political question. Here it found the basis sufficient.
d.r: Judicial review of suspension, now written into Art. VII, Sec. 18.

art-iii-sec-16.x: Everyone has a right to have their case decided promptly — not only in courts, but also before quasi-judicial and administrative bodies.
k: Broader than the speedy-trial right of Sec. 14(2): applies to all stages and all bodies, including preliminary investigation.
Balancing test: length of delay, reasons for it, assertion of the right, and prejudice to the respondent.
Inordinate delay may warrant dismissal.
art-iii-sec-16.w: Justice delayed burdens respondents with anxiety, expense and lost evidence.
t: After Cagang v. Sandiganbayan, the respondent must timely assert the right. Delay is measured against the periods in the rules, and the burden shifts depending on whether those periods were exceeded.
q: How does Sec. 16 differ from the speedy-trial right in Sec. 14(2)?
State the four factors of the balancing test.

d.h: The Court laid down guidelines for inordinate delay. The case starts with the filing of a formal complaint. Delay is measured against time periods set by rules. If those periods are exceeded, the prosecution must justify the delay. The right must be timely invoked, and it can be waived.
d.r: The governing framework for this section.

art-iii-sec-17.x: No one can be forced to be a witness against himself. The State cannot compel you to give testimony that may incriminate you.
k: Covers testimonial compulsion only — compelling a person to communicate facts from his own mind.
Physical or mechanical acts (fingerprinting, photographs, paraffin tests, physical examination, DNA samples) are generally not covered.
In a criminal case the accused may refuse to take the stand at all. An ordinary witness must take the stand and may refuse only specific incriminating questions.
Immunity statutes may remove the privilege by granting immunity.
art-iii-sec-17.w: It protects human dignity and the accusatorial system: the State must prove guilt by its own evidence.
t: Being compelled to produce a handwriting specimen has been held testimonial (Beltran v. Samson). A physical examination is not (Villaflor v. Summers).
The privilege applies in administrative proceedings that are penal in character, such as disbarment or revocation of a licence.
q: Is a compelled urine or DNA sample covered?
May a respondent in a penal administrative case refuse to testify altogether?

d.h: Compelling the accused to write from dictation to furnish a handwriting specimen violates the privilege. Writing requires the use of the mind; it is not a purely mechanical act.
d.r: The testimonial / physical distinction.

d.h: A woman charged with adultery could be compelled to undergo a physical examination to determine pregnancy. The privilege bars testimonial compulsion, not the use of the body as evidence.
d.r: Physical evidence is outside the privilege.

art-iii-sec-18.x: No one may be detained solely because of his political beliefs and aspirations. Involuntary servitude in any form is prohibited, except as punishment for a crime of which the person has been duly convicted.
k: Detention solely for political beliefs is barred. Overt acts may still be punished.
Involuntary servitude is prohibited, with the exception of punishment for a crime after due conviction.
Other recognized exceptions in jurisprudence: compulsory military or civil service under law; posse comitatus; return to work orders in labor disputes affecting national interest.
art-iii-sec-18.w: Liberty of conscience and the abolition of forced labor.
t: A return-to-work order is not involuntary servitude.
q: Give two recognized exceptions to the ban on involuntary servitude.

art-iii-sec-19.x: Fines may not be excessive, and cruel, degrading or inhuman punishments may not be imposed. The death penalty may be imposed only for heinous crimes Congress defines for compelling reasons. Any death penalty already imposed was reduced to reclusion perpetua. Physical, psychological or degrading treatment of prisoners, or the use of substandard or inadequate penal facilities, must be dealt with by law.
k: Prohibits excessive fines and cruel, degrading or inhuman punishment.
Death penalty: only for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes, by Congress. RA 9346 (2006) prohibits its imposition.
Par. (2): law shall deal with the abuse of prisoners and substandard penal facilities.
t: A penalty is not cruel merely because it is severe. It must be flagrantly disproportionate or shocking to the moral sense.
Under RA 9346, where the law prescribes death, reclusion perpetua (or life imprisonment) is imposed, without eligibility for parole.
q: What is the effect of RA 9346 on penalties of death?

art-iii-sec-20.x: No one may be imprisoned for failing to pay a debt or a poll tax.
k: “Debt” means a contractual obligation to pay money. It excludes liability arising from crime.
Poll tax is the community tax (cedula).
art-iii-sec-20.w: It prevents the revival of imprisonment for debt, a historic abuse against the poor.
t: BP 22 (Bouncing Checks Law) does not violate this section. It punishes the act of issuing a worthless check, not the failure to pay a debt (Lozano v. Martinez).
Estafa involving debts is punishable because of the fraud, not the debt.
q: Why is BP 22 not imprisonment for debt?

d.h: BP 22 was upheld. The gravamen of the offense is the act of making and issuing a worthless check, which harms public interest and the banking system. It is not the non-payment of an obligation.
d.r: Distinguishes penal liability for an act from imprisonment for debt.

art-iii-sec-21.x: No one may be put in jeopardy twice for the same offense. If an act is punished by both a law and an ordinance, a conviction or acquittal under either bars a prosecution under the other for the same act.
k: Requisites of first jeopardy: (1) a valid complaint or information; (2) a court of competent jurisdiction; (3) arraignment and plea; (4) conviction, acquittal, or dismissal/termination without the accused’s express consent.
Second sentence: protection against prosecution for the same act under a law and an ordinance.
The bar covers the same offense, an attempt or frustration of it, and offenses necessarily included in or including it.
art-iii-sec-21.w: Finality and fairness: the State, with its resources, may not wear down an individual by repeated prosecutions.
t: Dismissal on the accused’s own motion generally does not bar re-prosecution — except when the dismissal is on demurrer or for violation of speedy trial, which amounts to an acquittal.
Doctrine of supervening event: a later charge for a graver offense is allowed if the graver facts arose after the first plea (e.g., the victim dies).
q: List the requisites for the first jeopardy to attach.
Explain the “same act” rule in the second sentence.

d.h: An accused who was charged under a city ordinance for installing electric wiring devices without permit, and whose case was dismissed after arraignment, could not again be charged with theft of electricity under the RPC for the same act. The second sentence of the clause bars it.
d.r: Applies the “same act” rule between an ordinance and a national law.

art-iii-sec-22.x: Congress may not pass an ex post facto law or a bill of attainder.
k: Ex post facto law: one that makes criminal an act done before its passage which was innocent when done; aggravates a crime or increases its penalty retroactively; alters the rules of evidence to make conviction easier; or deprives the accused of a defense or protection to which he was entitled.
It applies only to criminal or penal matters.
Bill of attainder: a legislative act that inflicts punishment without judicial trial.
art-iii-sec-22.w: People must be able to rely on the law as it stood when they acted; punishment is for courts, not legislatures.
t: Procedural laws may apply retroactively if they do not prejudice the accused.
RPC Art. 22 makes penal laws favorable to the accused retroactive (except for habitual criminals).
q: Give the kinds of ex post facto laws.
Why was the Anti-Subversion Act not a bill of attainder?

d.h: The Anti-Subversion Act was upheld. It was not a bill of attainder because it did not single out persons for punishment without trial. Guilt still had to be established in court, including knowing and active membership with intent to further the party’s unlawful aims.
d.r: The leading Philippine case on bills of attainder.

art-i.x: The national territory: the Philippine archipelago, with all the islands and waters embraced in it, and all other territories over which the Philippines has sovereignty or jurisdiction — its land, sea and air, seabed, subsoil and insular shelves. The waters around, between and connecting the islands are internal waters.
t: The archipelagic doctrine: the islands and the waters between them form one unit.
RA 9522 (baselines law) was upheld in Magallona v. Ermita (2011): baselines are a tool to measure maritime zones under UNCLOS, not a way to give up territory.

art-ii-sec-1.x: The Philippines is a democratic and republican State. Sovereignty resides in the people and all government authority emanates from them.

art-ii-sec-2.x: The Philippines renounces war as an instrument of national policy, adopts the generally accepted principles of international law as part of the law of the land (incorporation), and adheres to peace, equality, justice, freedom, cooperation and amity with all nations.
t: Incorporation makes customary international law part of domestic law without any legislative act; treaties need Senate concurrence (Art. VII, Sec. 21).

art-ii-sec-3.x: Civilian authority is, at all times, supreme over the military. The armed forces protect the people and the State; their goal is to secure the sovereignty of the State and the integrity of the national territory.

art-ii-sec-6.x: The separation of Church and State shall be inviolable.
t: Read with Art. III, Sec. 5 (non-establishment and free exercise) and Art. VI, Sec. 29(2) (no public money for religion).

art-ii-sec-12.x: The State recognizes the sanctity of family life, protects the life of the mother and the life of the unborn from conception, and recognizes the primary right and duty of parents to rear the youth.

d.h: The Reproductive Health Law was upheld in the main, but provisions that compelled conscientious objectors to refer patients, punished them, or dispensed with spousal or parental consent were struck down. Life begins at fertilization.
d.r: The leading case on this section.

art-ii-sec-16.x: The State shall protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature.
t: Unlike most of Article II, this right is self-executing.

d.h: Minors, for themselves and for generations yet unborn, had standing to sue to stop timber license agreements: the right to a balanced and healthful ecology is enforceable even without an implementing law (intergenerational responsibility).
d.r: Self-executing environmental right.

art-ii-sec-26.x: The State guarantees equal access to opportunities for public service, and prohibits political dynasties as may be defined by law.
t: Not self-executing: there is no constitutional right to run for office, and the ban on political dynasties needs a law defining them (Pamatong v. COMELEC, 2004).

art-ii-sec-28.x: The State adopts and implements a policy of full public disclosure of all its transactions involving public interest, subject to reasonable conditions prescribed by law.
t: Read with the right to information, Art. III, Sec. 7.

art-iv-sec-1.x: Citizens of the Philippines are: those who were citizens when the Constitution was adopted; those whose fathers or mothers are citizens; those born before January 17, 1973 of Filipino mothers who elect Philippine citizenship upon reaching majority; and those naturalized in accordance with law.
t: The Philippines follows jus sanguinis (blood), not jus soli (place of birth).

art-iv-sec-2.x: Natural-born citizens are those who are citizens from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect their citizenship. Those who elect citizenship under Section 1(3) are deemed natural-born.

d.h: A foundling is presumed to be a natural-born citizen, given the high probability that her parents are Filipino and the generally accepted principles of international law.
d.r: Foundlings and natural-born status.

d.h: A natural-born citizen who lost citizenship and later reacquired it by repatriation recovers his original status as natural-born.
d.r: Effect of repatriation.

art-iv-sec-3.x: Philippine citizenship may be lost or reacquired in the manner provided by law.
t: RA 9225 (2003) lets natural-born Filipinos who became foreign citizens reacquire or retain Philippine citizenship by taking an oath, so that dual citizenship results.

art-iv-sec-4.x: Citizens who marry aliens keep their citizenship, unless by their act or omission they are deemed, under the law, to have renounced it.

art-iv-sec-5.x: Dual allegiance of citizens is inimical to the national interest and shall be dealt with by law.
t: Dual citizenship (an involuntary result of laws of two states) differs from dual allegiance (a person’s own act of loyalty to two states); only dual allegiance is prohibited (Mercado v. Manzano, 1999).

art-v-sec-1.x: Suffrage may be exercised by citizens not otherwise disqualified by law, at least eighteen years of age, who have resided in the Philippines for at least one year and in the place where they propose to vote for at least six months immediately before the election. No literacy, property or other substantive requirement may be imposed.
t: Registration is a procedural requirement, not a “substantive” one, so it is valid (Kabataan Party-List v. COMELEC, 2015, on biometrics).

art-vi-sec-1.x: Legislative power is vested in Congress (a Senate and a House of Representatives), except to the extent reserved to the people by initiative and referendum.
t: Non-delegation: Congress may delegate only if the law is complete and sets a sufficient standard.

art-vi-sec-3.x: A Senator must be a natural-born citizen, at least thirty-five years old on election day, able to read and write, a registered voter, and a resident of the Philippines for at least two years immediately before the election.

art-vi-sec-4.x: Senators serve six-year terms and may not serve more than two consecutive terms; voluntary renunciation is not an interruption.

art-vi-sec-5.x: The House has not more than 250 members unless the law provides otherwise, elected by district, plus party-list representatives who make up twenty percent of the total.

d.h: The two-percent threshold cannot bar parties from additional seats when the twenty-percent allocation is not filled; the Court laid down the formula for allocating party-list seats.
d.r: Party-list seat allocation.

d.h: Party-list groups need not represent marginalized sectors; national and regional parties may participate. New parameters were set.
d.r: Who may join the party-list system.

art-vi-sec-6.x: A Member of the House must be a natural-born citizen, at least twenty-five years old on election day, able to read and write, a registered voter in the district (except party-list), and a resident of it for at least one year immediately before the election.

art-vi-sec-7.x: Members of the House serve three-year terms and may not serve more than three consecutive terms.

art-vi-sec-11.x: Parliamentary immunity: members are privileged from arrest while Congress is in session for offenses punishable by not more than six years’ imprisonment, and may not be questioned elsewhere for any speech or debate in Congress or its committees.
t: The privilege from arrest does not cover offenses punishable by more than six years.
Speech and debate immunity protects against suits elsewhere, not against discipline by the member’s own chamber.

art-vi-sec-13.x: Incompatible and forbidden offices: a member may not hold any other government office (including in GOCCs) during his term without forfeiting his seat, nor be appointed to any office created, or whose pay was increased, during the term for which he was elected.

art-vi-sec-16.x: Each House elects its officers, determines its rules, and may punish members for disorderly behavior; suspension (not over sixty days) or expulsion needs the concurrence of two-thirds of all its members. A majority of each House is a quorum.

art-vi-sec-17.x: Each House has an Electoral Tribunal of nine: three Supreme Court Justices and six members of the House chosen on proportional representation. It is the sole judge of contests on the election, returns and qualifications of its members.
t: The tribunal’s jurisdiction begins once the winner has been proclaimed, has taken his oath and assumed office.

art-vi-sec-21.x: Congress or its committees may conduct inquiries in aid of legislation under duly published rules; the rights of persons appearing in or affected by them shall be respected.

d.h: An executive order requiring officials to secure the President’s consent before appearing in inquiries in aid of legislation was invalid in part; executive privilege must be invoked by the President or the Executive Secretary on her authority.
d.r: Limits of executive privilege.

d.n: Neri v. Senate Committee on Accountability
d.h: Presidential communications privilege protected an official’s answers to three questions on conversations with the President; the contempt and arrest order was set aside.
d.r: Presidential communications privilege.

art-vi-sec-22.x: Heads of departments may appear before either House on their own initiative or upon request; appearances in the question hour are conducted as the rules provide. Unlike Sec. 21, attendance here is discretionary.

art-vi-sec-23.x: Congress, by a vote of two-thirds of both Houses in joint session voting separately, has the sole power to declare a state of war; in times of war or other national emergency it may, by law, authorize the President to exercise powers necessary to carry out a declared national policy, for a limited period and subject to restrictions.

art-vi-sec-24.x: Appropriation, revenue and tariff bills, bills authorizing increase of the public debt, bills of local application, and private bills originate exclusively in the House; the Senate may propose or concur with amendments.

d.h: It is the bill, not the law, that must originate in the House. The Senate may propose a substitute bill once the House bill has been received.
d.r: What “originate exclusively” means.

art-vi-sec-25.x: Limits on appropriations: Congress may not increase the President’s budget recommendation; no rider; procedure for approving appropriations for Congress is strictly followed; no transfer of appropriations, but the heads of branches and constitutional bodies may augment items from savings in their own appropriations; and the general appropriations law is automatically re-enacted if not passed.

d.h: Acts under the Disbursement Acceleration Program were unconstitutional: withdrawn unobligated allotments were not “savings”, and cross-border transfers to other branches were prohibited.
d.r: Savings and augmentation.

d.h: The Priority Development Assistance Fund was unconstitutional: post-enactment intervention by legislators in the execution of the budget violates separation of powers and non-delegation.
d.r: The “pork barrel” case.

art-vi-sec-26.x: Every bill shall embrace only one subject expressed in its title. No bill becomes law unless it passed three readings on separate days and printed copies in final form were distributed three days before passage, except when the President certifies its immediate enactment to meet a public calamity or emergency.

art-vi-sec-27.x: Every bill is presented to the President, who signs it or vetoes it with his objections; Congress overrides the veto by two-thirds of all members of each House. The President may veto particular items of appropriation, revenue or tariff bills. A bill becomes law if he does not act within thirty days of receipt.

art-vi-sec-28.x: Taxation must be uniform and equitable; Congress shall evolve a progressive system. Charitable institutions, churches, parsonages and non-profit cemeteries, and all lands, buildings and improvements actually, directly and exclusively used for religious, charitable or educational purposes, are exempt from taxation. No tax exemption may be granted without the concurrence of a majority of all the members of Congress.
t: Sec. 28(3) exempts from property tax only (real property “actually, directly and exclusively used”), not from income tax.

section-29.x: No money may be paid out of the Treasury except under an appropriation made by law. No public money or property may be applied for the benefit of any religion or religious ministers, except to a priest or minister assigned to the armed forces, a penal institution, a government orphanage or leprosarium. Money collected on a tax levied for a special purpose is treated as a special fund.

section-30.x: No law may increase the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court without its advice and concurrence.

d.h: A law providing for direct appeal to the Supreme Court from the Ombudsman in administrative cases was void for increasing the Court’s appellate jurisdiction without its consent; such appeals go to the Court of Appeals.
d.r: Application of Sec. 30.

section-32.x: Congress shall provide for a system of initiative and referendum by which the people may directly propose and enact laws or approve or reject any act of Congress or local legislative body, upon a petition of at least ten percent of the registered voters, every district having at least three percent.
t: RA 6735 implements this for laws and local measures (not for constitutional amendments: Santiago v. COMELEC, 1997).

art-vii-sec-2.x: The President must be a natural-born citizen, a registered voter, able to read and write, at least forty years old on election day, and a resident of the Philippines for at least ten years immediately before the election.

art-vii-sec-4.x: The President and Vice-President are elected by direct vote for six years. The President is not eligible for any reelection; the Vice-President may not serve more than two successive terms. The Supreme Court en banc is the sole judge of contests on their election, returns and qualifications.
t: The Supreme Court sits as the Presidential Electoral Tribunal (PET) for these contests.

art-vii-sec-13.x: The President, Vice-President, Cabinet members and their deputies may not hold any other office or employment during their tenure unless the Constitution provides otherwise, nor practise a profession, engage in business or have financial interest in government contracts. The President’s relatives within the fourth degree may not be appointed to certain offices during his tenure.
t: This is stricter than the rule for other public officers (Art. IX-B, Sec. 7): other offices are allowed only if the Constitution itself provides (Civil Liberties Union v. Executive Secretary, 1991). Ex officio positions required by the primary function are not covered.

art-vii-sec-15.x: Two months before the next presidential election and until the end of his term, a President or Acting President shall not make appointments, except temporary appointments to executive positions when continued vacancies will prejudice public service or endanger public safety.

d.n: De Castro v. Judicial and Bar Council
d.h: The ban on midnight appointments does not apply to appointments to the Supreme Court, which Art. VIII, Sec. 4(1) requires to be made within ninety days of a vacancy.
d.r: Scope of the ban.

art-vii-sec-16.x: The President nominates and, with the consent of the Commission on Appointments, appoints heads of executive departments, ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, officers of the armed forces from the rank of colonel or naval captain, and other officers whose appointments are vested in him by the Constitution. Other officers are appointed without that consent.
t: Only the four groups named in the first sentence need confirmation (Sarmiento v. Mison, 1987).
Ad interim appointments during recess are effective at once, until disapproved or until the next adjournment of Congress.

art-vii-sec-17.x: The President has control of all executive departments, bureaus and offices, and shall ensure that the laws are faithfully executed.
t: Control (the power to alter or set aside a subordinate’s acts) differs from supervision over local governments (Art. X, Sec. 4).

art-vii-sec-18.x: As Commander-in-Chief, the President may call out the armed forces to prevent or suppress lawless violence, invasion or rebellion; and in case of invasion or rebellion, when public safety requires, may suspend the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus or place the country or part of it under martial law for not more than sixty days. He must report to Congress within forty-eight hours. Congress, voting jointly by a majority of all its members, may revoke it or, at his initiative, extend it. The Supreme Court may review the sufficiency of its factual basis in a proceeding filed by any citizen and must decide within thirty days.
t: Martial law does not suspend the Constitution, supplant civilian courts, or authorize military courts over civilians where civil courts function.
The suspension of the privilege applies only to persons judicially charged for rebellion or offenses connected with invasion.

d.h: Proclamation No. 216 (martial law in Mindanao) was upheld: the Court reviews only whether the President had sufficient factual basis, judged by what he knew at the time.
d.r: The standard of review under Sec. 18.

art-vii-sec-19.x: Except in impeachment cases or as otherwise provided, the President may grant reprieves, commutations and pardons, and remit fines and forfeitures, after conviction by final judgment; and may grant amnesty with the concurrence of a majority of all the members of Congress.
t: Pardon requires final conviction; amnesty does not.
Pardon for election offenses needs COMELEC’s favorable recommendation (Art. IX-C, Sec. 5).

art-vii-sec-21.x: No treaty or international agreement is valid and effective unless concurred in by at least two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.

d.h: The Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement was a valid executive agreement implementing existing treaties; it did not need Senate concurrence.
d.r: Treaties versus executive agreements.

d.n: Pimentel v. Office of the Executive Secretary
d.h: The President has the sole authority to ratify a treaty; courts cannot compel her to transmit a signed treaty to the Senate.
d.r: Who ratifies.

art-viii-sec-1.x: Judicial power is vested in one Supreme Court and lower courts. It includes the duty to settle actual controversies involving legally demandable and enforceable rights, and to determine whether there has been grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the government.
t: The second clause is the “expanded” certiorari jurisdiction, adopted to limit the political question doctrine.
Judicial review needs an actual case, standing, earliest opportunity, and the constitutional question as the lis mota.

art-viii-sec-4.x: The Supreme Court is composed of a Chief Justice and fourteen Associate Justices, sitting en banc or in divisions of three, five or seven. Cases on the constitutionality of a treaty, international or executive agreement, or law are heard en banc and decided by a majority of the members who actually took part and voted.

art-viii-sec-5.x: Powers of the Supreme Court: original jurisdiction over cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and petitions for certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, quo warranto and habeas corpus; review of judgments of lower courts in specified cases; temporary assignment of judges; change of venue; rule-making on pleading, practice and procedure, admission to the practice of law, the Integrated Bar and legal assistance; and appointment of court officials.
t: Rules of procedure must not diminish, increase or modify substantive rights.

d.h: Section 23 of RA 9165, which barred plea bargaining in drug cases, was unconstitutional: plea bargaining is a rule of procedure within the Court’s exclusive rule-making power.
d.r: Congress cannot legislate procedure.

art-viii-sec-7.x: A member of the Supreme Court must be a natural-born citizen, at least forty years old, and must have been for fifteen years or more a judge of a lower court or engaged in the practice of law. Members of the judiciary must be of proven competence, integrity, probity and independence.

art-viii-sec-9.x: Members of the Supreme Court and judges of lower courts are appointed by the President from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the Judicial and Bar Council for every vacancy, within ninety days from submission of the list for lower courts.

art-viii-sec-11.x: Justices and judges hold office during good behavior until seventy years old or incapacity. The Supreme Court en banc may discipline judges of lower courts or order their dismissal by a majority of the members who actually took part and voted.
t: Justices of the Supreme Court are removed only by impeachment (Art. XI, Sec. 2).

art-viii-sec-12.x: Members of the Supreme Court and other courts may not be designated to any agency performing quasi-judicial or administrative functions.

d.h: A judge could not serve as a member of a provincial committee on justice, an administrative body, consistent with the separation of powers.
d.r: Judges and administrative work.

art-viii-sec-14.x: No decision shall be rendered without expressing clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based. No petition for review or motion for reconsideration may be refused due course or denied without stating the legal basis.
t: Minute resolutions denying petitions for review are allowed: they adopt the findings below and state the basis briefly.

art-viii-sec-15.x: Cases must be decided within twenty-four months from submission in the Supreme Court; twelve months in lower collegiate courts, unless reduced by the Supreme Court; and three months in all other lower courts.

art-ix-sec-1.x: The Constitutional Commissions — the Civil Service Commission, the Commission on Elections and the Commission on Audit — are independent.

art-ix-sec-5.x: The Commissions enjoy fiscal autonomy: their approved annual appropriations are automatically and regularly released.

art-ix-sec-7.x: Each Commission decides by a majority vote of all its members any case or matter before it within sixty days from submission. Unless provided otherwise, its decisions may be brought to the Supreme Court on certiorari within thirty days from receipt of a copy.
t: The remedy is certiorari under Rule 64 (in relation to Rule 65), not an appeal.
COMELEC decisions in division must first be reviewed en banc before going to the Supreme Court.

art-ix-sec-2-2.x: The civil service embraces all branches, subdivisions, instrumentalities and agencies of the Government, including GOCCs with original charters. Appointments are made according to merit and fitness, determined as far as practicable by competitive examination, except for positions that are policy-determining, primarily confidential or highly technical. No officer or employee may be removed or suspended except for cause provided by law. Civil servants may not engage in electioneering or partisan political campaigns, and have the right to self-organization.
t: GOCCs without original charters (incorporated under the Corporation Code) are not in the civil service; their employees are under the Labor Code.

art-ix-sec-6-2.x: No candidate who lost in an election may, within one year after it, be appointed to any office in the Government or GOCCs.

art-ix-sec-7-2.x: No elective official may be appointed or designated to any public office during his tenure. Unless allowed by law or by the primary functions of his position, no appointive official may hold any other office.

art-ix-sec-8-2.x: No public officer or employee may receive additional, double or indirect compensation unless specifically authorized by law, nor accept any present, emolument, office or title from a foreign government without the consent of Congress. Pensions and gratuities are not additional compensation.

art-ix-sec-2-3.x: Powers of the COMELEC: enforce and administer election laws; exclusive original jurisdiction over contests on the election of regional, provincial and city officials, and appellate jurisdiction over contests of municipal and barangay officials decided by trial courts; decide all questions affecting elections except the right to vote; deputize law enforcement agencies; register parties; file petitions to include or exclude voters; investigate and prosecute election offenses; recommend measures to Congress; and recommend sanctions against its deputies.
t: Its decisions in contests involving municipal and barangay officials are final, executory and not appealable, but still open to certiorari.
The power to prosecute election offenses is now concurrent with the DOJ prosecutors (RA 9369).

art-ix-sec-5-3.x: No pardon, amnesty, parole or suspension of sentence for violation of election laws may be granted by the President without the favorable recommendation of the COMELEC.

art-ix-sec-9.x: Unless the COMELEC fixes otherwise in special cases, the election period begins ninety days before election day and ends thirty days after.

art-ix-sec-2-4.x: The Commission on Audit examines, audits and settles all accounts on the revenue and receipts of, and expenditures or uses of funds and property owned or held in trust by, the Government, including GOCCs with original charters, and on a post-audit basis entities with fiscal autonomy and non-governmental entities receiving subsidies. It has exclusive authority to define the scope of its audit and to promulgate accounting and auditing rules.

art-ix-sec-3-4.x: No law may exempt any entity of the Government or its subsidiaries, or any investment of public funds, from the jurisdiction of the Commission on Audit.

art-x-sec-2.x: Territorial and political subdivisions enjoy local autonomy.
t: Autonomy means decentralization of administration, not of power, for ordinary LGUs; autonomous regions enjoy political autonomy.

art-x-sec-4.x: The President exercises general supervision over local governments.

d.h: An order withholding part of the LGUs’ internal revenue allotments was invalid: supervision means seeing that local governments act within the law, not controlling them.
d.r: Supervision, not control.

art-x-sec-5.x: Each local government unit has the power to create its own sources of revenue and to levy taxes, fees and charges, subject to guidelines and limits Congress provides, consistent with local autonomy.

art-x-sec-6.x: LGUs have a just share, as determined by law, in the national taxes, automatically released to them.

d.h: The LGUs’ share must be computed on all national taxes, not only national internal revenue taxes as the Local Government Code’s wording had been applied; the base includes customs duties and other national taxes.
d.r: The “Mandanas ruling” on the just share.

art-x-sec-8.x: The term of elective local officials, except barangay officials, is three years, and no official may serve more than three consecutive terms. Voluntary renunciation of office for any length of time is not an interruption.
t: An involuntary loss of office (e.g., losing an election protest before the term ends) can interrupt; preventive suspension does not (Aldovino v. COMELEC, 2009).

art-x-sec-10.x: No province, city, municipality or barangay may be created, divided, merged, abolished or its boundary substantially altered except under the criteria in the Local Government Code and with the approval of a majority of the votes cast in a plebiscite in the political units directly affected.

art-xi-sec-1.x: Public office is a public trust. Public officers and employees must at all times be accountable to the people, serve them with utmost responsibility, integrity, loyalty and efficiency, act with patriotism and justice, and lead modest lives.

art-xi-sec-2.x: The President, the Vice-President, the Members of the Supreme Court, the Members of the Constitutional Commissions and the Ombudsman may be removed by impeachment for culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust. Other officers may be removed as provided by law, but not by impeachment.

art-xi-sec-3.x: The House has the exclusive power to initiate impeachment: a verified complaint by a member, or by a citizen with a member’s endorsement; a vote of at least one-third of all its members impeaches. No impeachment proceeding may be initiated against the same official more than once within a period of one year. The Senate has the sole power to try and decide; conviction needs two-thirds of all its members. Judgment extends only to removal from office and disqualification, but the convicted official remains liable to prosecution.
t: Proceedings are “initiated” when a complaint is filed and referred to the House Committee on Justice (Francisco v. House of Representatives, 2003).
When the President is on trial, the Chief Justice presides but does not vote.

art-xi-sec-12.x: The Ombudsman and his Deputies, as protectors of the people, shall act promptly on complaints against public officials and employees, including those of GOCCs, and notify the complainants of the action taken.

art-xi-sec-13.x: Powers of the Ombudsman: investigate any act or omission of a public official that appears illegal, unjust, improper or inefficient; direct officials to perform their duties; direct the officer concerned to take action against an erring official (including removal, suspension and other sanctions) and ensure compliance; request assistance; audit through COA; publicize matters; and recommend measures.
t: The Ombudsman’s power to impose administrative penalties is mandatory, not merely recommendatory (Office of the Ombudsman v. Masing, 2008).

art-xi-sec-15.x: The State’s right to recover properties unlawfully acquired by public officials or employees from them or their nominees or transferees is not barred by prescription, laches or estoppel.
t: This applies to civil actions for recovery of ill-gotten wealth, not to criminal prosecution (Presidential Ad Hoc Fact-Finding Committee v. Desierto, 1999).

art-xi-sec-17.x: A public officer or employee must submit, on assumption of office and as required by law, a sworn statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN). For the President, Vice-President, Cabinet, Congress, the Supreme Court, the Constitutional Commissions and other constitutional offices, and officers of the armed forces with general or flag rank, it is disclosed to the public as provided by law.

d.h: Quo warranto lay against the Chief Justice: her failure to file SALNs showed lack of proven integrity, a qualification for the office, so her appointment was void.
d.r: SALN and integrity.

art-xii-sec-2.x: Regalian doctrine: all lands of the public domain, waters, minerals, forests and other natural resources belong to the State; with the exception of agricultural lands, they may not be alienated. Their exploration, development and utilization are under the State’s full control and supervision, and it may enter into co-production, joint venture or production-sharing agreements with Filipino citizens or corporations at least sixty percent Filipino-owned, for up to twenty-five years, renewable for not more than twenty-five years. For large-scale exploration of minerals, petroleum and other mineral oils, the President may enter into agreements with foreign-owned corporations involving technical or financial assistance.

d.n: La Bugal-B’laan Tribal Association v. Ramos
d.h: Financial and technical assistance agreements with foreign-owned corporations are valid under Sec. 2(4) and may involve more than mere technical or financial assistance, provided the State keeps control.
d.r: Foreign participation in mining.

art-xii-sec-3.x: Lands of the public domain are classified into agricultural, forest or timber, mineral lands, and national parks. Only agricultural lands may be alienated. Private corporations may not hold alienable lands of the public domain except by lease (up to twenty-five years, renewable for up to twenty-five, and not more than one thousand hectares). Citizens may lease up to five hundred hectares, or acquire up to twelve hectares by purchase, homestead or grant.
t: Corporations may own private lands (if 60% Filipino), but may not acquire alienable public lands except by lease.

art-xii-sec-7.x: Save in cases of hereditary succession, no private lands may be transferred or conveyed except to individuals, corporations or associations qualified to acquire or hold lands of the public domain.
t: Aliens may acquire private land only by hereditary (intestate) succession; a sale to an alien is void (Krivenko v. Register of Deeds, 1947).
Former natural-born citizens may acquire limited private land (Sec. 8; BP 185 and RA 8179).

art-xii-sec-10.x: Congress shall reserve certain areas of investment to Filipino citizens or corporations at least sixty percent Filipino-owned, or higher as it prescribes. In granting rights, privileges and concessions covering the national economy and patrimony, the State shall give preference to qualified Filipinos.

d.h: The Filipino First policy is self-executing: a qualified Filipino bidder who matched the winning foreign bid for a controlling stake in the Manila Hotel, part of the national patrimony, had to be preferred.
d.r: Self-executing economic nationalism.

art-xii-sec-11.x: A franchise or authorization to operate a public utility may be granted only to Filipino citizens or to corporations at least sixty percent of whose capital is owned by Filipinos, for not longer than fifty years. Foreign participation in the governing body is limited to its proportionate share of the capital, and all executive and managing officers must be Filipino citizens.
t: “Capital” means shares entitled to vote in the election of directors (Gamboa v. Teves, 2011; Roy v. Herbosa, 2016).
RA 11659 (2022) narrowed what counts as a “public utility”, opening sectors like telecommunications and transport to full foreign ownership.

art-xii-sec-16.x: Congress shall not create private corporations by special law; government-owned or controlled corporations may be created by special charters in the interest of the common good and subject to the test of economic viability.

art-xii-sec-17.x: In times of national emergency, when the public interest requires, the State may, during the emergency and under reasonable terms it prescribes, temporarily take over or direct the operation of any privately owned public utility or business affected with public interest.
t: The power is exercised by Congress, or by the President only under a law delegating it (David v. Macapagal-Arroyo, 2006).

art-xiii-sec-3.x: The State shall afford full protection to labor, promote full employment and equality of opportunity, and guarantee the rights to self-organization, collective bargaining and negotiations, and peaceful concerted activities including the right to strike in accordance with law. Workers are entitled to security of tenure, humane conditions of work, a living wage, and participation in policy and decision-making processes affecting their rights and benefits.
t: The Constitution also recognizes the right of enterprises to reasonable returns on investment, and to expansion and growth.

art-xiii-sec-4.x: The State shall undertake an agrarian reform program founded on the right of farmers and regular farmworkers who are landless to own directly or collectively the lands they till, subject to priorities, retention limits and just compensation.

art-xiii-sec-18.x: Powers of the Commission on Human Rights: investigate all forms of human rights violations involving civil and political rights; adopt its operational guidelines; cite for contempt; provide legal measures and assistance; visit jails; establish education programs; recommend measures; and grant immunity from prosecution to witnesses.

d.n: Cariño v. Commission on Human Rights
d.h: The CHR has no adjudicatory power: it may investigate, but it cannot try and decide cases, such as the dismissal of striking teachers.
d.r: Investigate, not adjudicate.

art-xiv-sec-3.x: Religion may be taught, at the option expressed in writing by the parents or guardians, within the regular class hours in public elementary and high schools by instructors designated or approved by the religious authorities, without additional cost to the Government.

art-xiv-sec-4.x: Educational institutions, other than those established by religious groups and mission boards, shall be owned solely by Filipino citizens or corporations at least sixty percent Filipino-owned. Control and administration must be vested in Filipino citizens.

art-xiv-sec-5.x: Academic freedom shall be enjoyed in all institutions of higher learning. The State shall assign the highest budgetary priority to education.
t: Highest budgetary priority is not an absolute command: Congress may also fund debt service and other needs (Guingona v. Carague, 1991).
Institutional academic freedom covers who may teach, what may be taught, how, and who may be admitted to study.

art-xv-sec-2.x: Marriage, as an inviolable social institution, is the foundation of the family and shall be protected by the State.

art-xvi-sec-3.x: The State may not be sued without its consent.
t: Consent may be express (by law) or implied (when the State enters into a contract in its proprietary capacity, or itself sues). Suability is not liability: even when suable, public funds cannot be garnished without an appropriation.
A suit against an official is a suit against the State if it would require an affirmative act from the State or a charge on public funds.

art-xvi-sec-6.x: The State shall establish and maintain one police force, national in scope and civilian in character, administered and controlled by a national police commission.

art-xvi-sec-11.x: The ownership and management of mass media are limited to Filipino citizens or corporations wholly owned and managed by Filipinos. The advertising industry is limited to Filipinos or corporations at least seventy percent Filipino-owned.

art-xvii-sec-1.x: Any amendment to, or revision of, the Constitution may be proposed by Congress upon a vote of three-fourths of all its members, or by a constitutional convention.

art-xvii-sec-2.x: Amendments may also be directly proposed by the people through initiative upon a petition of at least twelve percent of the total number of registered voters, every legislative district being represented by at least three percent of its registered voters. No amendment may be proposed this way within five years after the ratification of the Constitution nor oftener than once every five years.
t: People’s initiative covers amendments only, never revisions (Lambino v. COMELEC, 2006).
Santiago v. COMELEC (1997): RA 6735 is inadequate to implement initiative on the Constitution.

art-xvii-sec-3.x: Congress may, by a vote of two-thirds of all its members, call a constitutional convention, or by a majority vote of all its members, submit to the electorate the question of calling one.

art-xvii-sec-4.x: Amendments or revisions are valid when ratified by a majority of the votes cast in a plebiscite held not earlier than sixty days nor later than ninety days after their approval (by Congress or the convention) or after certification of the sufficiency of the initiative petition.

art-xviii-sec-25.x: After the 1947 Military Bases Agreement expired in 1991, foreign military bases, troops or facilities may not be allowed except under a treaty duly concurred in by the Senate and, when Congress so requires, ratified by a majority of votes in a national referendum, and recognized as a treaty by the other contracting State.

d.h: The Visiting Forces Agreement was valid: it was concurred in by the Senate, and the United States treats it as a binding international agreement.
d.r: Visiting troops.
